title: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)
hook: "visiting relatives can be boring" means two things at once. the Brahma Sutra's third line does too, and Shankara keeps both
carry: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana and the post in the fog: doing has choices, but knowing depends on the thing. Where did you find a question you couldn't settle by deciding? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-five.

Visiting relatives can be boring. Hear that one more time. Is it boring to go and visit them? Or are the relatives who come to visit you the boring ones? The words don't change. The meaning flips. Often a sentence like that is a small accident. But a very short text, packed as tight as a seed, can carry two meanings on purpose, or at least leave room for both. The Brahma Sutra's third line is tiny. Shankara reads it two ways, one after the other, and doesn't throw either away. Today: the line about the source.
screen: `VISITING RELATIVES CAN BE BORING.` → `SAME WORDS, TWO MEANINGS.` → `A SHORT LINE, READ TWICE.`

segments.voice: The third line says, in effect: because of being the source of scripture. The key word is yoni, which means a source, a womb, a place things come from. And the compound can be read in two directions. First reading: Brahman is the source of scripture. Shankara points to the great Vedic texts, the Rig Veda and the rest, which shine on all kinds of things like a lamp. Texts like that, he says, can only come from something all-knowing. A source always knows more than what flows from it. He leans on the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, where the Vedas are described as the breathing out of a great being, as easily as breath. So the line says: look at the scriptures, and you'll know their source is no small thing. Second reading: scripture is the source, meaning the way of knowing Brahman. Here the line answers yesterday's worry. You can't reach Brahman by the senses, and reasoning alone can't settle it. So how is it known? Through the scriptures, the Upanishads above all. Scripture is the doorway by which jnana arrives. Shankara gives the first reading, then the second, and lets both stand. One says where the texts come from. The other says what the texts are for. Other Vedanta schools comment on this line in their own ways. For a jnana path, the double reading carries a quiet lesson. The source of what is known and the means of knowing it may turn out to be closer than they look.
screen: `YONI: A SOURCE, A WOMB.` · `BRAHMAN, THE SOURCE OF SCRIPTURE.` · `SCRIPTURE, THE WAY TO KNOW BRAHMAN.` · `BOTH READINGS STAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: follow one breath back to where it starts. Settle, and breathe naturally. Notice the out-breath, the way it leaves without effort. Then notice the small pause before the next breath begins. Rest your attention there, at the source, where the breath hasn't started yet. Don't hold the breath. Just notice the turning point, again and again. If you pray, you can let each out-breath be an offering. The bell holds the time.
Jnana. Knowing. On the third line, Shankara finds two directions: Brahman as the source of scripture, and scripture as the way jnana arrives. Today's word.

Your line: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening, Shankara's commentary, one point one point one to one point one point four. Today, when a sentence lands two ways, hold both readings for a moment before choosing. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Vedanta schools treat the Upanishads as the means of knowing Brahman, so their students study these texts closely, often with a teacher and alongside a commentary.

sources.ref: Brahma Sutra 1.1.3 (because of being the source of scripture)
Shankara, Brahma Sutra Bhashya 1.1.3 (two readings: Brahman the source of the Rig Veda and the rest, which illumine all things like a lamp; scripture the means of knowing Brahman)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.10 (the Rig Veda and the rest are the breathing out of the great being)

notes: Paraphrase of Shankara on 1.1.3: first reading, Brahman is the source (yoni) of the extensive scripture which, like a lamp, illumines all things, and only an omniscient being could be its source, with Brihadaranyaka 2.4.10 cited; second reading, scripture is the source (means of right knowledge) of Brahman. Confirm order and the lamp image.
'A source always knows more than what flows from it' compresses Shankara's argument that the author of a text knows more than the text contains. Confirm.
The sutra is the compound shastra-yonitvat; the spoken text calls it only tiny.
Other schools' readings of 1.1.3 are not described; confirm 'in their own ways' is fair.
Editor pass: 'Read that sentence again' (wrong for audio) now 'Hear that one more time'; cut the unsourced comparative claim that other schools treat scripture 'with equal seriousness'.
